problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=2t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=6t-3$ with respect to the inner product.

activity_context.topic_title: Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Inner Product Spaces

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace
examples.problem:
Let $V = \Bbb R_1[t],$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $1$ with real coefficients. Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
\langle p(t), q(t) \rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1),
$$

find the distance between $p(t) = 4t + 2$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t) = t$ with respect to the inner product.
examples.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $p(t)$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{ q(t) \}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t) & =\frac{⟨p(t),q(t)⟩}{⟨q(t),q(t)⟩}\,q(t) \\  & =\frac{p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)}{q(0)^{2}+q(1)^{2}}\cdot q(t) \\  & =\frac{(2)(0)+(6)(1)}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot t \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

The distance between $p(t) = 4t + 2$ and the subspace spanned by $q(t) = t$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖p(t)-{\text{proj}}_{q(t)}\,p(t)‖ \\  & =‖(4t+2)-6t‖ \\  & =‖-2t+2‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨-2t+2,\text{ }-2t+2⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-2t+2,\text{ }-2t+2⟩ & =(-2t+2){|}_{0}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{0}+(-2t+2){|}_{1}\cdot (-2t+2){|}_{1} \\  & =(-2(0)+2)^{2}+(-2(1)+2)^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d = \sqrt{4} = 2.$

feedback.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2},\,g(t)=\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}$ equals $3t.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=3t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)$ is an odd function, while ${t}^{2}$ is even. Hence, their product ${t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-1,1],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot {t}^{2}=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =3t+0 \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$
